description: The sit-up is a core-dominant exercise that trains the rectus abdominis, hip flexors, and obliques through hip flexion from a supine (lying) position. Proper form requires the core to do the work — not the neck, not momentum, and not the feet. A well-executed sit-up goes through the full range of motion from flat-back lying to fully upright, controlled in both directions.
cues: Lie flat with knees bent at about 90 degrees — feet flat on the floor
Cross your arms over your chest or place fingertips lightly behind your ears — do not pull your head
Breathe out hard and drive your belly button toward your spine to begin the curl
Your lower back should peel off the floor like a scroll — segment by segment
Pause at the top for one second when your elbows nearly touch your knees
Lower back down slowly — fight gravity all the way down, that is half the exercise
rules: Engage the core to lift the torso — do not pull the neck
Keep feet grounded on the floor throughout
Move in a controlled, smooth motion — no jerking
Keep the neck neutral — chin neither tucked to chest nor jutting forward
Control the descent — do not flop back down
Maintain left-right symmetry — do not twist or rotate
constraints: Do not pull the neck with hands — neck should be relaxed
Do not use momentum — the core must do the work
Avoid lifting feet off the floor
Avoid shallow reps — reach fully upright at the top

neck_pulling.cause: Using the hands to yank the head and neck forward instead of using the abdominals to curl the torso up.
neck_pulling.consequence: Cervical strain and potential disc injury. Also means the abs are NOT doing the work — making the exercise pointless.
neck_pulling.fix: Place hands lightly on your temples without gripping. The neck should be completely relaxed. If your neck hurts, your core is too weak — do less range of motion until you build strength.

using_momentum.cause: Swinging the arms forward or bouncing up from the floor to generate upward force.
using_momentum.consequence: The core is bypassed at the critical initiation phase — the hardest part of the movement — giving you zero benefit for that phase.
using_momentum.fix: Exhale and begin the curl by pressing the small of your back into the floor first. Initiate slowly. If you must swing, reduce range of motion.

feet_lifting.cause: Hip flexors too tight or too dominant — when the core cannot generate enough force, the hip flexors take over and pull the feet up.
feet_lifting.consequence: Hip flexors rather than abs become the primary mover — strains the lumbar spine and defeats the purpose.
feet_lifting.fix: Anchor your feet under a sofa or use a sit-up board. Focus on curling from the chest, not lifting from the hips.

shallow_range.cause: Stopping the ascent before reaching a fully upright position — usually due to fatigue or habit.
shallow_range.consequence: The abdominal muscles are never fully contracted. You are only training the first third of the movement.
shallow_range.fix: Pause at the top when your torso is fully upright and your elbows are near your knees. That is the full contraction position.

jerky_motion.cause: Fatigue causing loss of control, or rushing reps.
jerky_motion.consequence: Sudden force changes stress the spine at the thoraco-lumbar junction — a common source of back pain.
jerky_motion.fix: Take at least 2 seconds on the way up and 2 seconds lowering back down. Smooth is strong.

asymmetry.cause: Oblique imbalances or habit of rotating toward one side during the curl.
asymmetry.consequence: Develops asymmetric core strength. If done repeatedly, creates postural imbalances.
asymmetry.fix: Focus on your nose pointing straight at the ceiling throughout the movement. Record yourself from the front to check for any rotation.

tilt.note: Tracks the torso lifting angle through the full sit-up range

acceleration.note: Spike indicates momentum-driven movement — should stay moderate

gyro.note: Rotation/asymmetry indicator — should be near zero

stability.note: Stability is naturally lower during situps — trend matters

symmetry.note: Core twist detection via left-right sensor comparison
